description: We are a group of students whose interest represents diversity . From game dev to OSINT to even Designing , We have it all. We will love to use these skills to make students understand better.
summary:
We built Space Relics, a 3D website that tells the stories of the machines people have left on the Moon, on Mars and in deep space. Users pick a world and fly around it. They can click a marker or pick an object from a list, and the camera takes them there. Then a short story tells them why the machine was sent, what it did, and why it is still there.

Our site has 26 objects, such as the Apollo 11 lander, the Opportunity rover and Pioneer 10. We wrote every story in simple words that a school student can understand, and we added links to NASA sources for every story.

We believe these machines are not just junk. Each one is a part of human history. Our project helps people find them, learn about them and remember them.
details:
We made Space Relics, a website where users can explore the Moon, Mars and deep space in 3D. Our idea came from Google Earth. In Google Earth, people can spin the globe, zoom in and visit any place on Earth. We wanted to give people the same feeling, but for space. So we built something like Google Earth for the Moon, Mars and deep space, where users can fly to the real places where old machines were left and learn their stories.

We put markers in each place to show where these machines are today. When a user clicks a marker, the camera flies to it and a story panel opens. The story tells why the machine was sent, what it did and why it was left there. We also show some fun facts and links to our sources. Right now our site has 26 objects. On the Moon we have 10, like the Apollo landers, the Surveyor landers and the Soviet Lunokhod rovers. On Mars we have 9, like the Viking landers, Spirit, Opportunity, InSight and the Ingenuity helicopter. In deep space we have 7, like Pioneer 10, Pioneer 11, Voyager 1 and the Kepler and Spitzer telescopes.

We made the Moon and Mars as 3D globes using real maps, and we placed each marker using the real latitude and longitude of the machine. Deep space is shown as a simple map of the solar system. Users can move around with the mouse, touch or keyboard. We also added a search box and a counter that shows how many objects a user has explored. To build all this we used HTML, CSS and JavaScript, with Three.js for the 3D graphics. The Moon maps come from NASA's Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter. Our code is on GitHub and the website is hosted on Vercel.

We think our project can help students and teachers learn space history in a fun way. The stories are short and easy to read, and every fact has a source link so people can check it. The site works in a normal web browser, so users do not need to install anything.

We also wanted to be honest about our data. Each object has a label that says how sure we are about its place. It can be Confirmed, Approximate or Illustrative. Our 3D models are simple drawings and not exact copies, and we say this clearly on the site.

What makes our project creative is that we turned reading into a journey. Most people read about space missions in long articles. On our site, users fly to the real place first and then read the story there. We also added Voyager 1, which is still working, so users can see the difference between a machine that is alive and one that has gone silent.

While building it, we tried to keep the words simple so young people can understand. We checked our facts with NASA pages. We made the controls easy on both computer and phone, and we built the site in a way that lets us add more objects later
